title: What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify?From Activations to Interventions

paper.title: What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify? From Activations to Interventions
paper.abstract: Abstract Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are typically discovered from how their activations co-vary with behaviour, yet they are often used through interventions such as steering or ablation. We take intervention attribution, the first-order effect of a specified intervention on the model output, as our estimand. For a broad class of response functions, we show that observational feature-discovery evidence generally does not identify this attribution, and derive an exact gradient-based decomposition of the gap between linear-probe predictions and intervention attribution. Across four model-SAE pairs, median probe-to-attribution magnitude ratios range from tens to hundreds, while attributions closely track small-step steering. For single-latent ablations with nonzero effects, gradient predictions match the realized sign in 91–97% of cases, compared with 17–35% for probe-implied changes. Attribution-selected sets also produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than sets selected by correlation, rank tests or probe coefficients. Together, these results establish intervention attribution as a principled, gradient-estimable target for selecting SAE features for intervention.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) rewrite a language model’s activations as sparse combinations of thousands of latent features ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Huben et al., 2024 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) . Practitioners discover the features behind a behaviour observationally. They rank latents by how their activations co-vary with the behaviour across natural prompts, using correlations, class-mean differences or per-latent tests ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ; Patel et al., 2026 ; Cho et al., 2026 ) . They then use the selected features through interventions that promote or remove a concept, suppress an answer or correct a failure ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Marks et al., 2025 ; Arad et al., 2025 ) . Steering adds a multiple of a decoder direction ( Chalnev et al., 2024 ) , ablation zeroes a latent’s activation or replaces it with a reference mean ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) , and patching transplants it from another prompt ( Vig et al., 2020 ) . A specified intervention calls for a specified estimand. Its first-order effect averaged over prompts, α ( Δ ) = 𝔼 [ Δ ( H ) ⊤ ∇ F ( H ) ] \alpha(\Delta)=\mathbb{E}[\Delta(H)^{\top}\nabla F(H)] , is the intervention attribution , or attribution for short. Attribution patching computes it with one backward pass per prompt ( Nanda, 2023 ; Syed et al., 2024 ) . The estimand is intervention-specific and local. A finite effect also depends on how the gradient changes along the edit path. We therefore test it against realized interventions. Small-step steering checks its local accuracy, larger steps map its range of validity and single-latent ablations give a second check. Our first question is whether observational discovery evidence identifies α ⁡ ( Δ ) \alpha(\Delta) . In general, it does not ( Proposition 1 ). Natural prompts reveal F F only along the activation variation they realize. Two response functions can induce the same observational law while differing in slope along an unexplored direction, leading to different attributions for interventions that move along that direction. Unless the admissible response class rules out this variation, the attribution remains unidentified from observational evidence. This boundary applies to any functional of the observational law, including FDFI scores, correlations, rank tests, class-mean differences and probe coefficients, both at the population level and under the empirical law of the observed prompts. In our evaluation strata, the median fraction of the mean steering edit lying outside the observed activation span is nearly one, making this boundary directly relevant to the finite evaluation design we study. Proposition 1 concerns observational discovery statistics in general. Theorem 1 then studies a canonical way to translate observational association into an intervention-scale prediction using a linear least-squares probe. A discovery score such as an FDFI statistic ranks latents but does not quantify how much the output should change under a specified edit. Regressing the output on a latent’s activation yields such a prediction, which we call the probe-implied change ρ ⁡ ( Δ ) \rho(\Delta) . We use this probe as a common observational benchmark for comparing association with intervention attribution. For a fixed scalar activation and target, a correlation determines the probe coefficient after rescaling, as does a class-mean difference for a binary target ( Section B.3 ). Our second question is why ρ ⁡ ( Δ ) \rho(\Delta) and α ⁡ ( Δ ) \alpha(\Delta) differ once gradients are computed. Their difference splits exactly into three terms ( Theorem 1 , Table 1 ). A Stein residual compares the slope that the probe fits across prompts with the model’s average local sensitivity. An omitted-variable term compares the activation pattern that moves with the probe score with the coordinates that the intervention changes, for instance at another token position. An edit-gradient covariance arises when the size of the edit and the model’s sensitivity vary together across prompts, as for ablations. For example, a probe that reads only the final position implies no change for zero-ablating a latent that never fires there, whatever its attribution ( Corollary 1 ). One backward pass per prompt makes every term estimable. Our third question is whether this distinction matters in practice ( Section 5 ). Across four model-SAE pairs, it does in three ways. First, the gap is large. For FDFI-selected directions, the attribution is only a few percent of the probe coefficient in the median. The mismatch extends beyond FDFI-based selection: for latents selected by coefficient magnitude, probe coefficients exceed realized small-step steering responses by more than two orders of magnitude in the model-specific medians. Second, attribution predicts realized interventions. It closely tracks small-step steering and remains more accurate than the probe coefficient at displacements scaled to each latent’s maximum observed activation. Prompt-specific gradient predictions also substantially outperform probe-based predictions for single-latent ablations. Third, the distinction affects feature choice. Within FDFI-selected candidates, attribution more often identifies the latent with the largest realized steering response than either the FDFI statistic or the probe coefficient. Attribution-selected sets also produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than sets selected by correlation, rank tests or probe coefficients. Our contributions address these three questions. • Identification. We establish an identification boundary showing that observational feature-discovery evidence does not in general identify the first-order effect of a specified intervention ( Section 3 ). • Diagnosis. We derive an exact gradient-based decomposition of the gap between the probe-implied change and intervention attribution into three estimable terms, separating regression, omitted-variable and edit-gradient effects ( Section 4 ). • Intervention consequences. Across four public model–SAE pairs spanning GPT-2, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1 and an eleven-task setup, we show that the gap is large in practice. The proposed intervention attribution target predicts realized steering and single-latent ablations more accurately than probe-based predictions and attribution-based selection identifies latents with larger held-out intervention effects ( Section 5 ). Related work. Attribution patching estimates patching effects from one backward pass ( Nanda, 2023 ; Syed et al., 2024 ) , with refinements for attention saturation, integrated gradients and second-order terms ( Kramár et al., 2024 ; Hanna et al., 2024 ; Zhang and Wang, 2026 ) . Marks et al. (2025) use it to discover and intervene on sparse feature circuits, whereas we use it as the estimand against which observational evidence is judged. Empirical studies find that activation-side and output-side evidence about latents rarely coincide ( Arad et al., 2025 ; Shu et al., 2025 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Selection-error control ( Candès et al., 2018 ; Enkhbayar, 2025 ) and ablation-only validation ( Khera, 2026 ) leave the intervention’s attribution untested. Probing studies separate what a representation encodes from what a probe learns ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) or what the model uses ( Elazar et al., 2021 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . Our identity makes this separation exact for linear probes.

sections.text: Setup. We study four public model-SAE pairs, GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) and Llama-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , each with a residual-stream SAE at one layer ( Bloom, 2024 ; Lieberum et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ) . Eleven tasks cover factual recall (country capitals in free and multiple-choice form, country languages, birthplaces and occupations), lexical tasks (antonyms and last letters), in-context tasks (few-shot induction and indirect object identification) and arithmetic (simple addition and two-digit subtraction) ( Section D.1 ). The antonym task, with no evaluation stratum of at least three prompts, enters only the two-prompt ablation sensitivity analysis and the held-out set-ablation comparison. Unless stated otherwise, quantities are estimated on the held-out evaluation split within strata of at least three prompts, in within-task standard deviations of the log-probability ( Section D.1 ). Stratum-level t t intervals use a many-strata normal approximation ( Theorem C.1 ) and in simulation at the observed stratum sizes cover near the nominal level for the ablation terms and below it for the Stein residual ( Section C.2 ). Other intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals. The fixed-direction analysis, the coefficient-selected steering and the single-latent ablations are prespecified. The maximum-activation steering and the set-ablation comparison of selection rules are post hoc, specified after the aggregate results and before evaluation. The probe-to-ablation breakdown, the averaged-summary analysis, the ranking comparison and the worked example are post hoc ( Section D.2 ). For FDFI-selected directions under unit steering, the median ratio of attribution to probe-coefficient magnitude is 2.8 2.8 to 4.6 % 4.6\% across models, with the ratio below 10% for most pairs ( Table 2 ). This mismatch is not specific to FDFI. When we instead select 10 active latents per task by selection-split coefficient magnitude, their coefficients exceed realized small-step steering quotients by more than two orders of magnitude in the model-specific medians. The decomposition points to why: under both selections, the Stein residual and omitted-variable term are each comparable in magnitude to the coefficient. The discrepancy also persists beyond the final-position probe. In a post hoc descriptive analysis, probes on position-averaged decoder scores and FDFI’s averaged-code input remove most of the blindness to unread positions yet still overstate the attribution in aggregate ( Section E.5 ). Finally, sampling-noise analyses and prespecified robustness variants support the same qualitative conclusion ( Sections E.3 and E.1 ). Where the gap arises. Ablation interventions reveal how the terms in Corollary 1 arise in SAE pipelines. On GPT-2 and the Gemma models, about a third of FDFI-selected pairs have a non-negligible attribution but a zero or negligible probe-implied change ( Figure 2 B, Table 2 ). Almost all of these latents never fire at the final position, which is the only position read by the probe. For these pairs, the gap arises at unread positions and is dominated by the omitted-variable term, with the edit-gradient covariance accounting for much of the remainder ( Figure 2 C, Section E.4 ). More broadly, under zero-ablation, the covariance term C j C_{j} exceeds the mean-activation term in magnitude for a substantial share of selected pairs ( Section F.1 ). Predicting realized interventions. We first test whether attribution predicts realized interventions in the local regime. For coefficient-selected directions, we steer held-out prompts by a quarter of a within-stratum standard deviation of the latent score. The unit-direction attribution closely matches the realized central difference quotient T T and is closer than the probe coefficient for every pair ( Figure 2 A, Table 2 , Section E.2 ). We next examine how far this first-order approximation remains accurate by increasing the steering displacement for FDFI-selected directions. At a displacement scaled to each latent’s maximum observed activation, attribution agrees in sign with T T for nearly all pairs and remains closer than the coefficient for almost all. At five times this scale, the approximation breaks down for most pairs, with T T differing from the attribution by more than half its magnitude. Single-latent ablations provide an independent check. Prompt-specific gradient predictions have lower mean absolute error than probe-based predictions on every model and substantially higher sign agreement among ablations with nonzero realized effects ( Table 2 , Section F.2 ). Choosing latents for intervention. The gap affects feature choice as well as effect prediction. Within FDFI-selected candidates, attribution more often ranks first the latent with the largest realized steering response than either the FDFI statistic or the probe coefficient ( Section G.1 ). This agreement is nearly universal at small displacements and remains strong at a displacement scaled to the latent’s maximum observed activation, before weakening as the first-order approximation breaks down at larger scales. We then ask whether this advantage carries over to held-out feature selection. Using training folds to select up to 10 latents per task, attribution-selected sets produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than correlation-, rank-test- or coefficient-selected sets in every model-task unit ( Section G.2 ). These contrasts remain positive after normalization by edit norm and their two-stage intervals exclude zero. Attribution-selected sets also exceed class-mean-difference sets in most units. Compared with FDFI selection, the contrast is positive in most units and in three of four models.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Observational discovery and intervention attribution answer different questions. Empirical studies report that activation-side evidence about latents need not predict their effects under intervention ( Arad et al., 2025 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ) . We formalize this separation with an intervention-specific estimand, an identification boundary within the response class of Proposition 1 and an exact decomposition ( Theorem 1 ). In the evaluated pipelines the gap changes which latents one would choose. Discovery statistics remain useful for finding candidate features, whereas claims about the consequence of a specified intervention rest on evidence about that intervention. In a white-box model one backward pass per prompt computes the empirical attribution. For each such intervention one can report its attribution with a held-out interval, the terms of ( 5 ) and the share of the mean edit outside the observed span. Scope and extensions. The attribution is the first-order effect of a specified intervention. Whether a latent is the sole mechanism behind a behaviour or necessary or sufficient for it is a broader mechanistic question. The identity holds for any layer, dictionary, linear readout and intervention that keeps the SAE error term. Our experiments cover four model-SAE pairs at one layer each and eleven tasks, with few selected pairs for Llama-3.1-8B, teacher-forced outputs and steering up to five maximum activations. Two directions follow. For inference, the stratum-level construction targets a fixed-weight population attribution under independent sampling across strata ( Appendix C ). Inference over template clusters would relax that independence. Anytime-valid confidence sequences under adaptive intervention sampling ( Asiaee, 2026 ) suggest a route to inference for adaptively chosen interventions. For finite effects, the intervention must also be evaluated at the scale of interest. Downstream nonlinearities can make first-order approximations inaccurate ( Zhang and Wang, 2026 ) , motivating identification and inference beyond local attribution.

sections.text: Appendix B proves the results of the main text, reads the terms of the probe-to-intervention identity and extends Corollary 1 to any set of edited positions. This appendix states that design, proves the many-strata inference and assesses coverage by simulation. Assumption 2 (Split design) . (i) (Independence) The SAE, the active set, the selections, the summaries and the edits are fixed by data independent of the evaluation split ( Cox, 1975 ; Rinaldo et al., 2019 ) . The evaluation prompts are independent draws from each task’s law. (ii) (Moments) Within each evaluation stratum the activations, the targets and the gradients have finite second moments. sections.text: Stratum-specific quantities are estimated without bias in strata with at least three prompts and pooled within task with weights ω k ∝ n k − 1 \omega_{k}\propto n_{k}-1 ( Proposition C.1 ). A ratio such as a probe coefficient is the ratio of its pooled numerator and its pooled denominator ( Section E.1 ). Pooling prompts over strata before estimation would change the estimand, since the coefficient of a probe pooled over all strata of a task splits exactly into a within-stratum and a between-stratum part. Over the 50 50 , 244 244 , 481 481 and 24 24 selected direction-task pairs the median absolute share of the between-stratum part is 0.632 0.632 , 0.816 0.816 , 0.818 0.818 and 0.662 0.662 . A pooled probe is thus mostly a contrast between answers and prompt lengths, which is why every estimate is computed within a stratum.

sections.heading: D.2 Prespecified and post hoc analyses
sections.text: The fixed-direction analysis and its variants ( Section E.1 ), the coefficient-selected steering and its second-dictionary replication ( Sections E.2 and E.2 ), the ablation decomposition ( Section F.1 ) and the single-latent ablations ( Section F.2 ) are prespecified. A prespecified analysis has its estimand and decision rule fixed before its outcome is computed. Three further prespecified criteria of these plans concern set ablations. The first requires the prompt-specific gradient prediction of the finite ablation of each task’s selection to be more accurate than the probe-based one. It is met in all four models under zero- and mean-ablation, with paired intervals excluding zero. Each of the other two must hold in at least three models. The second requires the first-order regime at reduced edit scales of the set ablation, with a near-quadratic remainder of slope in [ 1.5 , 2.5 ] [1.5,2.5] . It is met in all four models. The third requires interactions to dominate the remainder of the full set ablation, with an interaction share above 0.5 0.5 . It is met only on Gemma-2-9B. The remaining analyses are post hoc and designed after the aggregate results. They comprise the larger steering steps and the maximum-activation displacements ( Section E.2 ), the sampling-noise analysis ( Section E.3 ), the probe-to-ablation breakdown and the positional analysis ( Sections E.4 and E.4 ), the probes on FDFI’s averaged summaries ( Section E.5 ), the observed span of a stratum with its prespecified readout ( Section D.4 ), the rankings against steering responses and the held-out set ablations ( Appendix G ) and the worked example ( Appendix H ). sections.heading: Appendix F Ablation terms and realized intervention effects
sections.text: This appendix supports the statements of Section 5 that the covariance term in the attribution of an ablation is of the order of its mean-activation term and that gradient-based first-order predictions of realized single-latent ablations agree in sign with the realized effect far more often than probe-based ones. Section F.1 splits the attribution of each ablation into its two terms and Section F.2 compares first-order predictions of single-latent ablations with their realized effects. Every intervention keeps the SAE error term and acts at every position but the first. Zero-ablation sets the latent’s code to 0 0 and mean-ablation to its selection-split task mean. The ablation terms L j L_{j} , M j M_{j} and C j C_{j} of ( 7 ) are estimated within strata of at least three prompts and pooled with weights n k − 1 n_{k}-1 . Intervals are 95 % 95\% percentile bootstrap intervals with 2,000 2{,}000 replicates, whose resampling unit each caption states.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: For each selected latent j j and task, L j L_{j} , M j M_{j} and C j C_{j} are estimated unbiasedly within every stratum. The edit is the one applied in the realized ablations of Section F.2 , the latent’s code times its unnormalized decoder row and, where the SAE release defines one, its activation scaling factor. Under mean-ablation the code is replaced by its deviation from the reference mean.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text:
The covariance term is of the same order as the mean term. Under zero-ablation, | C j | > | M j | |C_{j}|>|M_{j}| for 52 52 , 34 34 , 39 39 and 17 % 17\% of direction-task estimates. Adding C j C_{j} reverses the sign of M j M_{j} for 26 26 , 17 17 , 18 18 and 4 % 4\% . The median share | C j | / ( | M j | + | C j | ) |C_{j}|/(|M_{j}|+|C_{j}|) is 0.511 0.511 , 0.381 0.381 , 0.375 0.375 and 0.267 0.267 , with upper deciles of 0.635 0.635 to 0.851 0.851 ( Table F.1 ). The fraction with | C j | > | M j | |C_{j}|>|M_{j}| is stable when strata of two prompts are admitted. Under mean-ablation it is larger on three models and nearly equal on GPT-2, with C j C_{j} reversing the sign of M j M_{j} for 13 13 to 20 % 20\% . The definitions of Corollary 1 explain the large shares. sections.heading: Appendix G Choosing latents for intervention
sections.text: This appendix supports the paragraph of Section 5 on choosing latents. Both analyses rank or select latents and then compare the choice with realized intervention effects. The first ranks the FDFI-selected latents of the steering extension of Section E.2 . The second selects sets of latents on training folds and ablates them on held-out prompts.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: The units are the model-task pairs of the steering extension with at least two FDFI-selected latents ( 6 6 , 9 9 , 9 9 and 4 4 units, 28 28 in total). The analysis counts the units in which the latent with the largest steering response is ranked first by the FDFI statistic ϕ ^ l / se ^ l \hat{\phi}_{l}/\widehat{\rm se}_{l} of Section D.3 , by the coefficient magnitude | β | |\beta| or by the attribution magnitude | α | |\alpha| . The primary target is the central difference quotient | T | |T| , the response per unit displacement. A second target is the finite half-difference | ε ​ T | |\varepsilon T| of the positive and negative steering interventions, not a one-sided intervention effect, with β \beta and α \alpha scaled by the same latent-specific step ε \varepsilon . Uniformly random choice within each unit matches the target in 3.31 3.31 units in expectation. This expectation serves as a reference. The analysis is post hoc. Because the attribution and T T use the same evaluation prompts, the agreement is descriptive. Section G.2 gives a held-out comparison.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The FDFI statistic and coefficient magnitude seldom rank first the latent with the largest quotient magnitude within the selected candidate set ( Table G.1 ). With the scaled target the coefficient’s ranking gains at large steps, because the step sizes differ across latents. sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: The units are the model-task pairs whose FDFI selection holds at least three latents ( 5 5 , 10 10 , 10 10 and 3 3 units, 28 28 in total). They use the up to 200 200 evaluation prompts per task of the set-ablation design in five folds, including prompts excluded by the primary stratum-size restriction and the antonym task. Correlation, rank-test, class-mean-difference and coefficient scores are computed on the four training folds. Attribution sets also use those folds. The FDFI comparator uses the selection-split statistic of Section D.3 . Every rule selects k t = min ⁡ ( 10 , | S t | ) k_{t}=\min(10,|S_{t}|) latents from the active pool. The rules are the absolute correlation between the position-averaged code and the target, the absolute statistic of a Mann-Whitney test between the upper and lower target terciles, the absolute class-mean difference between those terciles, the magnitude | β | |\beta| of the within-stratum pooled final-position coefficient over training strata with at least two prompts, the FDFI selection of Section D.3 and the attribution set. The attribution set maximizes the training-fold first-order set effect | ∑ j ∈ K L j | |\sum_{j\in K}L_{j}| over sets K K of k t k_{t} active latents. Each set is zero-ablated on the held-out fold at every position but the first, keeping the SAE error term. The primary contrast is d c ≔ A attr − A c d_{c}\coloneqq A_{\rm attr}-A_{c} , where A A is the absolute held-out mean finite effect in standardized units, averaged over folds and then equally over units. Intervals resample strata within model, task and fold. A two-stage version resamples tasks within model and then strata. Both use 2,000 2{,}000 replicates and hold the fitted selections fixed. The comparison is post hoc, specified after the aggregate results and before evaluation ( Section D.2 ).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Attribution sets produce larger held-out ablation effects than correlation, rank-test and coefficient sets in every unit, with two-stage intervals excluding zero ( Table G.2 ). They exceed class-mean-difference sets in most units, with a two-stage interval that excludes zero at the 95 % 95\% level but not after a Bonferroni correction over the five comparators. Against the FDFI selection the contrast is positive on three models and in most units, but its two-stage interval includes zero. The two rules are therefore not distinguished under task resampling. Coefficient sets have the smallest edit norms, consistent with latents that rarely fire on held-out prompts. After dividing the absolute held-out mean effect by the root-mean-square edit norm within fold and averaging, the attribution sets still exceed the correlation, rank-test and coefficient sets on every model. The comparison measures the effect on the answer’s log-probability. How a larger ablation effect translates into a better intervention depends on the downstream goal.
